content.readme:
# Rune A native GPU-rendered Rust UI framework for macOS, Windows, Linux and the web, with its own renderer, text, layout and springs. Every app can run headless, so an agent can render to PNG, dump the element tree and drive it with scripted input.

```rust fn view(s: &State, _: &mut Cx) -> El { let t = tok::theme(true); let label = text(if s.on { "Lights on" } else { "Lights off" }) .font(type_::TITLE).color(t.text); let knob = el().key("knob").size(18.0, 18.0).radius(9.0).fill(t.knob) .absolute(if s.on { 18.0 } else { 2.0 }, 2.0); let switch = el().key("switch").role("switch").label("Lights").checked(s.on) .focusable(true).size(38.0, 22.0).radius(11.0) .fill(if s.on { tok::accent(0, true) } else { t.control_off }) .motion(motion::SNAPPY) .on_press(|s: &mut State| s.on = !s.on) .child(knob); col().w_full().h_full().center().gap(16.0).fill(t.bg).child(label).child(switch) } ``` ## Use it with your agent Give your coding agent this repo. Have it start from [`examples/hello`](examples/hello) and [`crates/rune/README.md`](crates/rune/README.md), then check its own work headlessly by rendering PNGs and inspecting the element tree. > Build me a with Rune (github.com/anomalyco/rune). Start from examples/hello and check your work headlessly. ## Add it ```toml rune = { git = "https://github.com/anomalyco/rune", rev = "" } ``` Rune is pre-release. Pin a rev of `dev`; `dev` is never rewritten. On Windows, the MSVC toolchain (`x86_64-pc-windows-msvc`, rustup's default) needs only the Visual Studio C++ build tools rustup asks for. The GNU toolchain (`x86_64-pc-windows-gnu`) also needs MinGW-w64's binutils on `PATH`: `windows-link` (under `parking_lot`, `libloading`, `windows-core` and `windows-sys`, so under every Windows UI crate) imports with `raw-dylib`, rustc makes those import libraries with `dlltool` on GNU targets, and the `dlltool` in rustup's `rust-mingw` can't run without an `as` it doesn't ship ([rust-lang/rust#140704](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/140704)). Without binutils the build stops at `windows-result` with `error calling dlltool 'dlltool.exe': program not found`. Install [MSYS2](https://www.msys2.org), run `pacman -S mingw-w64-ucrt-x86_64-binutils`, and put `C:\msys64\ucrt64\bin` on `PATH` (or build with `RUSTFLAGS=-Cdlltool=C:\msys64\ucrt64\bin\dlltool.exe`). [Docs](crates/rune/README.md) · [Components](crates/rune-kit/README.md) · [Examples](examples) · [Changelog](CHANGELOG.md) ## Contributing We don't take pull requests. Have your agent [open an issue](https://github.com/anomalyco/rune/issues) describing the bug or idea, and our agents usually turn it around fast. MIT, © Anomaly.

content.readme:
HatchZip

Extract huge archives in place. The archive shrinks as your files hatch,
so you only need free space for the output, not for the output and the archive.

hatchzip.dev | Installation | Usage | Safety | How it works | Contributing

HatchZip is a free, open-source archive extractor for Windows, macOS and Linux, with a desktop app and a command line tool. It extracts ZIP, 7z, RAR, tar and split archives in place, for when there is not enough disk space to extract an archive next to itself, such as a large game download on a nearly full disk. Download it from [hatchzip.dev](https://hatchzip.dev). A 180 GB game download that unpacks to 200 GB needs 380 GB of disk with WinRAR, 7-Zip or `unzip`, because the archive and everything extracted from it have to exist at the same time. HatchZip needs a little over 200 GB. It extracts the archive from the end and cuts each finished part off the archive file as it goes, so the space the archive gives back is reused for the next files. It checks that the extraction will fit before it changes anything, keeps a safety margin of free space the whole way through, and can be stopped or crash at any moment and pick up where it left off. It reads ZIP, 7z, tar, `.tar.gz`, `.tar.bz2`, `.tar.xz`, RAR volume sets and split archives. ### Get it > [!IMPORTANT] > HatchZip is only distributed from this repository's [releases](https://github.com/xevrion/hatchzip/releases) and its site, [hatchzip.dev](https://hatchzip.dev). Other sites using the name, such as hatchzip.com, are not affiliated with this project. No coding needed. **[Download for Windows](https://github.com/xevrion/hatchzip/releases/latest/download/HatchZip-x64-setup.exe)** (Windows 10 and 11), or for [macOS (Apple Silicon)](https://github.com/xevrion/hatchzip/releases/latest/download/HatchZip-aarch64.dmg), [macOS (Intel)](https://github.com/xevrion/hatchzip/releases/latest/download/HatchZip-x86_64.dmg) and [Linux](#installation). 1. Run the installer. Windows may show "Windows protected your PC" because HatchZip is not code-signed yet: choose **More info**, then **Run anyway**. 2. Right-click the archive, choose **HatchZip**, then **Extract here**. On Windows 11 the menu is under **Show more options**. To pick the destination folder first, choose **Extract files…** instead. 3. Or open HatchZip from the Start menu, open the archive, and choose **Extract**. HatchZip shows whether the files will fit before it changes anything. The archive is used up as the files come out, so when it finishes, only the extracted files are left. **Extract here** puts an archive with one folder or one file at its top next to the archive. An archive with several files or folders at its top goes into a new folder named after it, so its files never mix with what is already there. The progress window closes when the extraction completes; to keep it open, clear **Close the progress window when extraction completes** in the app's Settings menu. To keep the archive when there is room for both, choose **Extract here (keep archive)** in the right-click menu. To always keep archives, as other extractors do, clear **Remove the archive during extraction** in the app's Settings menu; every right-click entry then keeps the archive too. That is a normal extraction: the archive is not changed, and space is required for all extracted files. ## When there is not enough disk space to extract The same 200 MB of game data (21 files), packed by the real tools, extracted on a 220 MiB disk with about 50 MB free: | Archive | `unzip` / 7-Zip | HatchZip | |---|---|---| | ZIP, 180 MB | `unzip` ran out of space at file 6 of 21 | Finished, every file byte-identical | | 7z from 7-Zip 25.01, `-ms=20m` (10 solid blocks) | Needs 380 MB | Finished in 0.64 s, every file byte-identical | | 7z split into 5 volumes of 40 MB

content.readme:
# Herdr

Herdr is a desktop app for terminals and coding agents. Keep work in spaces, see which agents need you, and leave terminals running when you close the window.

## Install

### Linux and macOS

```sh
curl -fsSL https://releases.herdr.dev/app/install.sh | sh
```

Linux needs a desktop session and a working Vulkan driver. macOS builds are available for Apple Silicon; Intel Mac users can [build from source](#build-from-source). Linux builds are x86-64 and ARM64.

The installer adds Herdr to your apps and puts the command in `~/.local/bin`.
Add that folder to your PATH if the installer asks.
On macOS the app lives in `~/Applications/Herdr.app`.
For drag-and-drop installation on Apple Silicon, download [Herdr.dmg](https://releases.herdr.dev/app/Herdr.dmg) and drag Herdr to Applications.

On macOS (Apple Silicon), you can also install with [Homebrew](https://brew.sh/):

```sh
brew install --cask herdr-app
```

### Windows

Run in PowerShell on x64 Windows with curl and tar installed (Windows 10 1803 or newer):

```powershell
irm https://releases.herdr.dev/app/install.ps1 | iex
```

Herdr appears in the Start menu. The installer adds `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\herdr-app` to your user PATH. Open a new terminal to pick it up.

The shell and PowerShell installers download and run code. Read the [shell installer](distribution/install.sh) or [PowerShell installer](distribution/install.ps1) first if you prefer.
They also install [herdr-core](https://github.com/herdrdev/herdr-core) if it is missing.
The app can help install or update a core it cannot use.

## Find your work

A **space** holds work on one machine, usually in one repo. Each space has **tabs**. Split a tab into **panes** to put terminals or mod panels beside each other.

An unnamed space follows its first terminal's folder. Name a space or tab when you want a label that stays.
New tabs start in the focused terminal's folder.

The agents sidebar brings agents from your spaces into one list, including workers started by another agent.
Agents that report status show as:

- **Working:** still busy.
- **Blocked:** waiting for you.
- **Done:** finished while you were looking elsewhere.
- **Idle:** not working, or a finished agent you have looked at.

Click an agent to see it. A worker without a pane opens in **peek**, over your tab. Keep it as a tab if you want it beside your other work.
Ctrl-click a live terminal address in terminal text to peek at it; use Cmd-click on macOS.
An address such as `t7` means a terminal on the same machine as the terminal showing it. `vps/t7` names one on another machine.

The window arranges terminals. The core runs them.
Closing the window leaves them running; closing a pane or tab ends its terminals.
After a reboot or core crash, kept panes get fresh shells in their last folders, not their old programs.

## Work on another machine

Add an SSH machine from Settings → Machines or the sidebar's Add machine action.
Pick a host from your SSH config or type how SSH reaches it.
Spaces on that machine run their terminals there, not on your computer.

Each machine keeps its spaces, tabs and splits in its core. Connected screens share that structure and the live terminals, but keep their own focus and zoom.
Remote work keeps running when your local window closes or your laptop sleeps, as long as the remote machine and core stay up.

## Make it yours

Open the command palette to find an action by name, or open Settings to change fonts, colors, sounds and other preferences.
Settings > Look also adjusts terminal line height and scroll speed. Both default to 100%; layouts can override them with `terminal_line_height` (0.8–2) and `terminal_scroll_speed` (0.1–5).
The built-in layouts include Herdr, Terminals and Herdr 98.
A **layout** arranges the window. **Mods** are small JavaScript programs that draw its panels, menus and dialogs.

Duplicate a shipped layout or mod before changing its structure or code. Your copies stay yours; Herdr updates the shipped ones on start.
Save a personal layout, mod or key file and the window reloads it.
A broken edit keeps the last good version and reports the error.

Ctrl+Shift+P shows every command and its key (Cmd+Shift+P on macOS). Change any key in `keys.json`; see [the keys section](defaults/AGENTS.md#keys-keysjson) of the mod guide for the format, including JSON objects for named, typed command arguments.

On macOS, Cmd+A selects the terminal's whole screen and scrollback, ready for Cmd+C.
In vim and other alternate-screen apps, it selects only that screen.
Linux and Windows keep Ctrl+A for the shell; bind `terminal.select_all` in `keys.json` if desired.

content.readme:
# Native Shell (NSH) **Build once, native everywhere.** Native Shell is a native UI framework for iOS, Android, macOS, Windows, Linux and the web, built in Rust. It unifies components, state, logic and API, with app-owned visual design and platform rendering: native views on iOS, Android, macOS, Windows and Linux, HTML on the web, GPUI in GPUI apps, character Cells in a terminal, with the platform's own text, input and interaction (a menu is a popup on the desktop and a sheet on a phone). Write the whole app in Rust, its screens in TSX, or combine both with shared Rust components. Package it as a standalone app on every platform, or embed it in an existing one. On the same engine, apps load TSX modules at run time — plugins, features, UI generated by AI — delivered as signed packages and run in a sandbox the host configures. Documentation, guides and live demos: **[nsh.dev](https://nsh.dev)**. ## Goals Native views and interaction, with an app-owned design: NSH shares components, state and APIs across platforms, while the app controls colors, typography, spacing, shapes and motion. `nsh/base` provides the behavior and accessible structure of common controls such as `Button`, `Checkbox` and `Switch`; apps and community libraries give them a look. Platform modules expose capabilities specific to their platforms, such as the mobile system tab bar. Read [Goals and design principles](https://nsh.dev/docs/goals) for the component boundaries and how these goals guide Rust apps, TSX modules and AI-generated UI. ## Features - Write apps in Rust, TSX, or both, and render with each platform's own UI, sharing the same reactive engine, flexbox and grid layout, system text, input and accessibility. - Give your app its own look: NSH provides the primitives, Tailwind classes, a theme and an unstyled UI foundation (`nsh/base`: navigation, safe areas, dialogs, the keyboard, the status bar), and your app draws its components from them in TSX or Rust. - Embed in existing native apps alongside components such as maps and web views, or package as standalone apps and static websites. - Deliver TSX screens at run time with signed packages and host-controlled sandbox capabilities. - Build AI-generated screens with TSX and Tailwind, generated TypeScript declarations and [model-readable documentation](https://nsh.dev/llms.txt). - Iterate with TSX hot updates, headless tracing and a single Rust-built `nsh` CLI for building and packaging. ### Platforms | Platform | Drawn with | Embed with | Requires | |---|---|---|---| | iOS | UIKit, CoreText | `NshAppView` (Swift, `NativeShell.xcframework`) | iOS 15+ | | Android | Android views, `StaticLayout` | `NshView` (Java / Kotlin, `nsh.aar`) | Android 8 (API 26)+ | | macOS | AppKit, Core Animation, CoreText | `AppView` (Rust, `nsh-platform-macos`) | macOS 14+ | | Windows | Win32, Direct2D, DirectWrite | `AppView` (Rust, `nsh-platform-windows`) | Windows 10 1809+ | | Linux | GTK 4, Pango | `AppView` (Rust, `nsh-platform-linux`) | GTK 4.14+ | | GPUI (macOS, Windows, Linux) | GPUI (GPUI Fast) | `AppView` (Rust, a GPUI view, `nsh-platform-gpui`) | macOS, Windows; Linux with Vulkan | | Terminal | ratatui, the terminal's Cell grid | `AppView` (Rust, an area of a ratatui frame, `nsh-platform-tui`) | Terminals on macOS, Windows, Linux | | Web | HTML, CSS | `createPlayer` (JavaScript) or an iframe | Modern browsers | Each desktop runs and packages apps with its own backend (AppKit, Win32, GTK 4). The GPUI backend draws with GPUI on all three desktops and embeds NSH in GPUI and GPUI Kit apps; `nsh run --target gpui` shows an app as they do. The web platform (`nsh run --target web`, `nsh package --target web`) publishes apps as static sites and runs the website's live demos. The terminal backend (`nsh run --target tui`) draws apps on a terminal's character grid in its own colors, with the keyboard and the mouse. ## Quick start Install the `nsh` command ([other ways](https://nsh.dev/docs/installation)):
macOS / Linux ```sh curl -fsSL https://nsh.dev/install.sh | sh ``` The nightly build of the latest `main`, rebuilt every night that it changes: ```sh curl -fsSL https://nsh.dev/install.sh | sh -s -- --nightly ```
Homebrew ```sh brew install longbridge/tap/nsh ```
Windows (PowerShell) ```powershell irm https://nsh.dev/install.ps1 | iex ```
From source (macOS / Linux) Build and install the latest `main` from source (Git, Rust and the [platform build dependencies](https://nsh.dev/docs/installation) required): ```sh curl -fsSL https://nsh.dev/install.sh | sh -s -- --source ``` Re-run to update. The checkout stays in `~/.nsh/source` for runtime builds.

basic_info.description: Incremental rust builds up to 92x faster than cargo/rustc

content.readme:
Rebuild Rust in milliseconds.

Type blaze wherever you'd type cargo.
Blazingly fast Rust, literally.

Install · Try it · How fast · How it works · Docs

## Install ```sh curl -fsSL https://ix.dev/blaze | sh ``` For macOS on Apple silicon and Linux, with or without Rust installed: blaze builds with its own Rust, whatever rustup or the project pins, and the installer downloads it once (about 125 to 160 MB; none when rustup already has that same nightly; v2's blaze cannot fetch it yet: [toolchain.md](docs/toolchain.md)). Rather use crates.io or Nix? [Other ways to install](docs/install.md). That installs **stable**: a release that passed the heavy tests (real projects on macOS and Linux: cargo, zed, servo, bun, NVIDIA Dynamo, fff, fframes, flox and OpenAI's Codex CLI each build, build again after an edit faster than with cargo, and pass their tests). **Canary** is the newest release, out as soon as it is built and promoted to stable unchanged once it passes them ([release.md](docs/release.md)): ```sh curl -fsSL https://ix.dev/blaze | sh -s -- --channel canary ``` ## Try it In any Rust project: ```text blaze run # like cargo run blaze test # like cargo test blaze build # like cargo build ``` The first build loads your project and compiles every crate of it, with no cargo build and no rustc. Then change a function and build again: blaze's daemon, still running, builds only what the edit changed. blaze answers `build`, `check`, `run`, `test` and `bench`; other cargo commands are not blaze's yet. ## How fast These numbers are blaze v1's; v2 has not been measured yet. - Edits rebuild **10× faster** on macOS arm64, **24× faster** on Linux aarch64 and **11× faster** on Linux x86-64 than with `cargo build`, on average over real projects. - **About 20 ms** from saving a file to a running program using the new code, with [live edits](docs/usage.md#change-a-running-program). | Edit one function, then build (Linux x86-64) | `cargo build` | `blaze build` | |---|---:|---:| | ripgrep | 508 ms | **56 ms** (9.1× faster) | | nushell | 1.25 s | **236 ms** (5.3× faster) | | helix | 2.15 s | **116 ms** (19× faster) | | bun (1.25M lines of Rust) | 9.11 s | **451 ms** (20× faster) | Every project, platform, chart, and the memory and disk it takes: [benchmarks](docs/benchmarks.md). ### Over time How blaze's own numbers move from run to run, each platform on its own benchmark machine: the instructions each merge to main retires, how long an edit takes and how soon a live edit runs, from [the history](docs/benchmarks/history) ([how it is kept](docs/benchmarks.md#history-and-regressions)). Every workflow that adds to the history draws these again and commits them with it. Not drawn until there are two runs on one machine: macOS arm64 instructions per merge (none yet), macOS arm64 edit times (one run), Linux aarch64 instructions per merge (none yet), Linux aarch64 edit times (one run), Linux x86-64 instructions per merge (none yet), Linux x86-64 edit times (one run), Windows x86-64 live-edit latency (one run). ## How it works blaze's daemon keeps your project compiled in memory, with no cargo or rustc under it. After an edit it compiles only the functions you changed and links the program again with its own linker. [More](docs/v2/plan.md). ## Good to know - **macOS on Apple silicon and Linux.** Windows has no installer, and v2 has not been run there ([v1 on Windows](docs/platforms.md#windows-x86-64-msvc)). - **blaze is its own toolchain.** It builds every project with its own Rust, `blaze-2026-10-27` (today the nightly of that date), whatever the project pins; stable code and `#![feature(...)]` code build. Your toolchain and CI stay the final word ([why](docs/toolchain.md)). - **It trades memory for speed:** a few GB for a small project. - **It's young.** Keep `cargo check` or your CI as the final word, and [tell us](https://github.com/indexable-inc/blaze/issues) when something

basic_info.description: the ultimate vocal synthesizer - sing, speak, beatbox, and more

content.readme:
# CHIMERA

A physical-modeling voice synthesizer in the browser. Every sound comes from a simulated
airway (lungs, vocal folds or syrinx, a branched vocal tract, lips, nose), not from samples.
The engine is Rust, compiled to WebAssembly for an AudioWorklet; the same code runs natively
for tests and the `chimera` CLI.

## Vision & scope

1. **One instrument**: a physically modeled voice (lungs, vocal folds, throat, mouth). No
   samples, no neural audio.
2. **The web app is the primary surface**: anyone should be able to make songs in it without
   an LLM's help. Mobile is the likely next surface. The plugin (CLAP/VST3/AU) still ships, but
   it's secondary.
3. **More realistic without losing what it is**: the robotic, primitive sound people like today
   stays available, and every realism change is checked by ear against it.
4. **Languages enter through one shared front-end design**, not one-off hacks. Each needs a
   native speaker's check and must leave English unchanged.
5. **The design language (the vector display) is settled**; the look within it can still evolve.
6. **Nothing copyrighted in git**; MIT; a deterministic, real-time-safe engine.
7. **Not now**: a DAW or sequencer, a light theme, MPE, multi-voice dialogue.

## What it does

- **Play**: drag the tongue, lips and jaw in a live cutaway of the head; vowel pad, encoders,
  computer keyboard and Web MIDI.
- **Speak**: English text (CMUdict with a letter-to-sound fallback) or IPA, turned into
  gestures and prosody, with the gestural score and a consonant chart on screen. In IPA mode a
  notice under the box lists the symbols and marks the voice doesn't say (`chimera render speech`
  prints the same as warnings).
- **Sing**: a pitch roll with lyrics per note; consonants land before the beat. Lyrics can be
  English or Korean (Hangul: one block per note, with Korean sound rules); each language is a
  front end ([docs/language-front-ends.md](docs/language-front-ends.md)).
- **Beatbox**: pads and a step sequencer, every drum an articulatory gesture.
- **Bestiary**: songbird (two-voice syrinx), seal, alligator and elephant.
- **Duet** (`?show=<id>`): two 3D heads replay a pre-rendered song.

Male, female and child bodies blend continuously. Everything on screen animates from live
engine state: pressure in the airway, airflow, the vocal folds, spectra and formants.

## Run it

Needs Rust with the `wasm32-unknown-unknown` target, and Bun.

```sh
bun install
bun run dev        # builds the wasm, then Vite on 127.0.0.1:5317
bun run test       # wasm build, cargo test --workspace, bun test tests
```

The AudioWorklet needs a secure context, so open it on localhost or over HTTPS (for example
`tailscale serve`). Vercel builds it with `vercel.json`.

Offline renders and measurement:

```sh
cargo run --release -p chimera-cli -- render speech|text|song|notes|beatbox|creature|vowels …
cargo run --release -p chimera-cli -- diagnose       # nasal leakage, formants, bandwidths, pitch
cargo run --release -p chimera-cli -- compare csd    # against a real singer (docs/csd-comparison.md)
cargo run --release -p chimera-cli -- compare tsp    # against 23 real speakers (docs/speech-comparison.md)
bun tools/spectrogram.ts in.wav out.png
bun tools/musicxml-to-notes.ts score.mxl P1 --out p1.json   # a score's part → `render notes` melody
```

## Docs

- [docs/architecture.md](docs/architecture.md): the acoustic model (FDTD airway, sources,
  anatomy, gestures), and its [references and credits](docs/architecture.md#references-and-credits).
- [docs/rust-engine.md](docs/rust-engine.md): the engine's real-time and determinism contract,
  and the browser boundary.
- [docs/ui-redesign.md](docs/ui-redesign.md) and [docs/mockups/](docs/mockups/): the vector
  display look.
- [docs/csd-comparison.md](docs/csd-comparison.md): scoring the voice against the Children's
  Song Dataset.
- [docs/speech-comparison.md](docs/speech-comparison.md): scoring the speech against real
  speakers, phone by phone (the TSP speech database).
- [docs/hill-climb/](docs/hill-climb/): the rules and log for tuning the voice one measured
  step at a time.

Agents: see [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md).

## License

[MIT](LICENSE). Bundled third-party files keep their own licenses: the CMU Pronouncing
Dictionary ([public/data/CMUDICT-LICENSE.txt](public/data/CMUDICT-LICENSE.txt)) and the fonts
([public/fonts/](public/fonts/)).

content.readme:
A tiny, fast container runtime for macOS, Windows and Linux.
Runs your Docker images and works with the docker CLI, Compose and buildx you already use.

Download · Features · Build from source · Releases

🇬🇧 🇮🇩 🇩🇪 🇪🇸 🇫🇷 🇮🇹 🇵🇱 🇧🇷 🇻🇳 🇹🇷 🇷🇺 🇸🇦 🇯🇵 🇰🇷 🇨🇳 🇹🇼
Kiri speaks 16 languages. Is yours one?

--- Kiri is a lightweight replacement for Docker Desktop and OrbStack, written in Rust. It runs containers in one small Linux VM (or straight on the kernel on Linux) and speaks the Docker Engine API, so your tools just work. The name comes from the Igbo word *ntakịrị*, "small". ## Why Kiri - **Fast**: a container starts and exits in about 2.5 ms through the Docker API. That's around 80 times faster than Docker Desktop. - **Light**: the VM sleeps after 60 s idle, the daemon stays at about 15 MB, and it wakes in about 0.15 s. - **Compatible**: `docker`, Compose, buildx, `docker login` and amd64 images through Rosetta. - **Local domains**: `http://.kiri.local`, with HTTPS from Kiri's own certificate authority. - **More than containers**: a one-command Kubernetes cluster and Linux machines. - **A native window** for containers, images, volumes and networks, plus a menu bar item. - **In your language**: 16 languages, on macOS, Windows and Linux alike. ### In your language Kiri's window and setup come in these languages. It follows your system's language, and you can change it in Settings → Appearance. In Arabic the whole window reads right to left. | | Language | | Language | | Language | | Language | |---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---| | 🇬🇧 | English | 🇫🇷 | Français | 🇻🇳 | Tiếng Việt | 🇯🇵 | 日本語 | | 🇮🇩 | Bahasa Indonesia | 🇮🇹 | Italiano | 🇹🇷 | Türkçe | 🇰🇷 | 한국어 | | 🇩🇪 | Deutsch | 🇵🇱 | Polski | 🇷🇺 | Русский | 🇨🇳 | 简体中文 | | 🇪🇸 | Español | 🇧🇷 | Português (Brasil) | 🇸🇦 | العربية | 🇹🇼 | 繁體中文 | Missing yours? Translations live in [`crates/kiri/src/ui/lang`](crates/kiri/src/ui/lang); see [Contributing](#contributing). ## Install | Platform | Get it | |----------|--------| | macOS 14+ (Apple silicon or Intel) | `.dmg` from [runkiri.com/releases](https://runkiri.com/releases/) | | Windows 10 and 11 (x86-64 or Arm, through WSL 2) | `.msi` from [runkiri.com/releases](https://runkiri.com/releases/) | | Linux (Ubuntu, Fedora and others) | `.deb` or `.rpm` from [runkiri.com/releases](https://runkiri.com/releases/) | The first time you open Kiri, it sets up a `kiri` Docker context. Kiri updates itself, and checks each new release's signature first. ## Quick start ```sh docker --context kiri run --rm alpine echo hello docker --context kiri compose up -d kiri k8s start # single-node Kubernetes as the `kiri` kubectl context kiri machine create dev --distro ubuntu && kiri machine shell dev kiri import # bring images, volumes and containers over from OrbStack or Docker Desktop ``` Docker's commands also work as `kiri` commands (`kiri run`, `kiri ps`, `kiri compose up`, and so on), and always target Kiri. ## Numbers `alpine` running `true` and removed, median of 30 runs, same `docker` CLI for all three: | | Docker Engine API | `docker` CLI | |----------------|------------------:|-------------:| | **Kiri** | **2.55 ms** | **14.2 ms** | | Docker Desktop | 213 ms | 243 ms | | OrbStack | 380 ms | 442 ms | Method and every other figure are in [`bench/results.json`](bench/results.json). Rerun with `kiri bench`. ## How it works ``` docker CLI ─┐ compose ────┼─ Docker Engine API ─► kiri daemon ── vsock ──► guest agent (PID 1) buildx ─────┤ owns the VM clone3 → container kiri UI ────┘ ``` The VM uses a custom 10 MB kernel, and its PID 1 is a ~900 KB Rust agent. That agent starts containers with a single `clone3` into namespaces

Quiet.md

A fast, quiet, local notes app.
Drawn natively with Rust + GPUI. Your notes stay on your computer, stored in the Feishu (Lark) DocxXML format.

English · 简体中文 · 日本語

   

Website · Download · Performance · Features · Contributing

content.readme:
# Reason Network

![Make your bots talk to your Claude Code and Codex.](assets/reason-network-banner.png)

Your agents, talking to your **teammates'** agents. End-to-end encrypted, peer to peer.

> **AI agent asked to join the Reason Network?** Follow https://reasonmachines.com/network

One small daemon per computer. Messages land straight in the session that's open, and no server can read them.

Every coding agent session on every teammate's computer shows up (who, which repo and branch, busy or idle, what it's
doing right now), and any of them can message the right one: Claude Code, Codex, Command Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI,
Copilot CLI, Grok CLI, opencode, pi, DeepSeek Harness and Reason.

## Get started

Paste this line to your coding agent (Claude Code, Codex, Command Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI, …):

```
Join the Reason Network: https://reasonmachines.com/network
```

Or run it yourself, in a terminal:

```sh
curl -fsSL https://reasonmachines.com/install.sh | bash -s -- network
```

How it works:

1. **Sign in, and you have a network.** Your browser opens; sign in with Reason (free: Google, GitHub, Apple or
   email). The coding agents on this computer are set up.
2. **Your other computers join by signing in with the same account.** Run the same line there; it lands on your network.
3. **Friends join with your invite line.** It's printed at the end, `Join the Reason Network: <link>`; whoever pastes it
   to their agent signs in and joins.

With an invite link, in a terminal:

```sh
curl -fsSL https://reasonmachines.com/install.sh | bash -s -- network join '<link>'
```

- **Hosted assistants** (Grok Bot, Muse, ChatGPT, …): add the MCP server `https://mcp.reasonmachines.com/mcp`.
- **Windows**, in PowerShell: `irm https://reasonmachines.com/network/install.ps1 | iex`

That's it. Ask any agent "who's on the network?", tell it to ask someone's agent something, or to send them a file.

Step-by-step guides:

- [Make Grok Bot talk to Claude Code](https://reasonmachines.com/network/grok-bot-claude-code)
- [Connect Muse to Claude](https://reasonmachines.com/network/muse-claude)
- [Make Codex and Claude Code talk to each other](https://reasonmachines.com/network/codex-claude-code), compared with the Codex plugin, agent-link-mcp and shared files
- [Grok Bot vs Muse vs Claude Duet vs Dots](https://reasonmachines.com/network/compare): what each is for, and how to connect them

## What you get

- **Every agent on the team.** Agents get `list_team`, `send_message`, `message_status` and `ask_user`, plus
  `check_inbox` where messages can't be pushed, under the MCP server `reason-network`. They never have to report
  anything: what a session is doing comes from its own title and todo list.
- **Messages reach each agent on its delivery path.** Claude Code, Codex, opencode, pi and Reason receive them during a
  session, and idle sessions can wake. Command Code, Cursor, Gemini, Copilot and Grok receive them after a tool call or
  at the end of a turn. DeepSeek Harness gets them when it checks its inbox. Every tool result says if mail is waiting.
  Existing Claude sessions join without a restart.
- **Native Antigravity conversations.** Setup installs its MCP configuration and native hooks. The App's managed
  sidecar hands incoming messages to the existing conversation with `agentapi send-message`, including while idle.
  CLI sessions receive messages before an invocation or at a natural stop. Hooks supply `session_id` for tools, so

content.readme:
Import .sql files into your TypeScript code with full type inference

Read the docs →


If you have a file like this: ```sql -- get_author.sql select u.id, u.name, count(p.id)::int as post_count from users u left join posts p on p.user_id = u.id where u.id = :id::int group by u.id ``` You can import it directly from a TypeScript file like this: ```ts // main.ts import postgres from "postgres"; import getAuthor from "./get_author.sql"; const db = postgres(process.env.DATABASE_URL); const author = await getAuthor.run(db, { id: 1 }); // { id: number; name: string; post_count: number } | null ``` Reylo is powered by TypeScript [content mappers](https://github.com/microsoft/typescript-go/pull/4712), introduced in TypeScript 7.1 (currently [in beta](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/typescript/announcing-typescript-7-1-beta/)), which let you dynamically define static types for external file types and integrate them directly into TypeScript compilation. Reylo is the perfect option for the agent era: - 💪 **The full power of SQL** — any syntax, function or operator your database supports - 🌵 **DRY** — no redundant hand-written types - 🎯 **Checked against your database** — a misspelled column is a type error - 🤖 **Agent-friendly** — DRY code is more maintainable for agents - 🧩 **Postgres, MySQL, SQLite and DuckDB** (preview) — Neon, PlanetScale, Cloudflare D1, Turso and more - 🔌 **Bring your own driver** — `pg`, postgres.js, `mysql2`, `better-sqlite3` and [more](#supported-drivers) - ⚡ **No codegen** — no generated files, no watcher ## Setup To install Reylo, you'll need: - **TypeScript 7.1 (currently in beta).** The first release with content mappers. - **Node 24 or later.** - **A running dev database.** Postgres, MySQL 8.0.22 or later, or a SQLite or DuckDB file: Reylo reads your current schema from it. Install Reylo, which brings its engine for your machine, and TypeScript 7.1: ```sh npm install reylo npm install -D typescript@beta ``` Add Reylo to `tsconfig.json`, for `.sql` files and for its project file, `.reylo.yaml` or `.reylo.yml`: ```jsonc // tsconfig.json { "compilerOptions": { /* ... */ }, "contentMappers": [ { "package": "reylo", "extensions": [".sql", ".reylo.yaml", ".reylo.yml"] } ] } ``` Then type-check with `--runExternalCode`, which lets `tsc` run content mappers: ```jsonc // package.json { "scripts": { "typecheck": "tsc --noEmit --runExternalCode" } } ``` Point Reylo at your dev database with `DATABASE_URL`, in your environment or in `.env`. Its scheme tells Reylo which database you use: ```sh # .env DATABASE_URL=postgres://localhost:5432/app # or mysql://…, file:./app.db for SQLite, duckdb:./app.duckdb for DuckDB ``` To make `.sql` imports work at run time too, load Reylo where your code runs. On Node: ```sh node --env-file=.env --import reylo/register main.ts ``` For Bun, Nub, Vite, Next.js, esbuild, webpack, Rspack, Cloudflare Workers and Jest, add [the plugin for your setup](https://reylo.dev/#plugins), or copy its complete [example project](https://github.com/colinhacks/reylo/tree/main/examples). To see the types as you type, set up [your editor](https://reylo.dev/#editors). To give your coding agent Reylo's rules for writing and running queries, install its skill: ```sh npx skills add colinhacks/reylo --skill using-reylo ``` ## Usage Write a query in a `.sql` file, import it, and run it with your database driver: ```sql -- get_user.sql select id, name, email from users where id = :id::int ``` ```ts import getUser from "./get_user.sql"; const user = await getUser.run(db, { id: 1 }); // { id: number; name: string; email: string | null } | null ``` Name each parameter with a colon, and give it a type with a cast where the query doesn't pin one down. Pass `.run()` your driver's client: a pool, a client, or a con

content.readme: # Oink — Oink Is Not only a KVM **English** | [简体中文](README.zh-CN.md) | [日本語](README.ja.md) | [한국어](README.ko.md) Oink, short for "Oink Is Not only a KVM", is modern software that builds a peer-to-peer sharing network across multiple Windows and Mac computers. Use the keyboard, mouse and trackpad of any device to control any nearby device, with the same native feel everywhere; play the audio of several devices through the speakers or headphones connected to one of them; share the clipboard and drag and drop between devices; discover devices on the local network automatically; all traffic is encrypted by default. ## Install Get installers and matching source from [GitHub Releases](https://github.com/oinkvm/oink/releases). Supported operating systems and versions: - **Mac:** Apple silicon (arm64), macOS 14.2+; Intel (x64), macOS 14.2+ (untested) - **Windows:** x64, Windows 10 version 1809 (build 17763) or later, or Windows 11. Windows 10 versions before 22H2 are untested. Windows 10 LTSC (such as LTSC 2019 / LTSC 2021) does not include the WebView2 Runtime; install the Microsoft Edge WebView2 Runtime (Evergreen) first: https://developer.microsoft.com/microsoft-edge/webview2/ If SmartScreen says "Windows protected your PC", use **More info → Run anyway** only if offered. UAC may show an unknown publisher. ### Sponsor If this project helps you, consider sponsoring some of my AI subscription costs. Those tokens help make Oink better. ## Contributing This project does not accept pull requests without context, because there is no one to review the code. Please use [Issues](https://github.com/oinkvm/oink/issues) for all bug reports and feature requests. When you report a problem, please include your device environment, diagnostic data, steps to reproduce and your AI-assisted investigation's conclusions. Using Oink in real environments and sending feedback is the biggest contribution to this project. ## FAQ **Is Oink based on, or compatible with, Deskflow?**\ No. Oink is a project started completely from scratch. It uses its own peer-to-peer (not client–server) protocol and is not compatible with other software KVMs. **Do I have to designate one device as the controller?**\ No. Oink uses a peer-to-peer design: the keyboard and mouse connected to any device can control the other devices. **Can I share trackpad gestures?**\ Yes, but trackpads on Windows have not been tested. **Does it support clipboard sharing and drag and drop across operating systems?**\ Yes. The clipboard is synced across devices automatically, and you can drag text, images and files directly from one device to another — even straight into apps such as Chrome. **Do I need to buy a license for personal or commercial use?**\ No. Oink is free software released under GPL-3.0-only with additional terms, so you can use it for any personal or commercial purpose without asking for any further license. If you distribute Oink or a modified version of it, you must provide the complete source code under the same license, keep the original author attribution and license notices, and mark your changes; under the additional terms you also may not use the Oink name to promote derived products. Modifying Oink only for your own use, without distributing it, carries none of these obligations. ## License This project is licensed under [GPL-3.0-only](LICENSE) with [additional terms](LICENSE-ADDITIONAL-TERMS.md).

# Ely Office

Offline-first desktop apps in Rust and GPUI. Files stay in your folders; no account, no cloud service.

Download from [office.elygpui.com](https://office.elygpui.com) or the [latest release](https://github.com/ELY-Open-Source/ElyOffice/releases/latest): Windows, macOS (Apple silicon and Intel) and Linux (AppImage, deb, rpm, Arch, Nix; Debian 11 and Ubuntu 20.04 or newer).

| App | Does | Engine |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ElyDoc | Word processing (DOCX, ODT) | LibreOfficeKit |
| ElyTable | Spreadsheets (XLSX, ODS, CSV) | LibreOfficeKit |
| ElyShow | Presentations (PPTX, ODP) | LibreOfficeKit, system media |
| ElyPDF | PDF reading and editing, OCR, signatures | MuPDF, Tesseract |
| ElyMail | Mail over IMAP, POP3 and SMTP; follows the system proxy | own IMAP and POP3, mail-send, SQLite |
| ElyTree | Git client | Git |
| ElyMark | Markdown | pulldown-cmark, RaTeX, mermaid-rs-renderer; MuPDF for PDF export |
| ElyAgent | Second release | Kigi CLI |

ElyMail signs in to Microsoft with OAuth, to Gmail and iCloud with an app password, and to QQ Mail, 163 and 126 with an authorization code.

Install Rust with [rustup](https://rustup.rs) (`rust-toolchain.toml` pins the version), then the system packages. Every system also needs Git, Python 3, curl, Node.js 22.18 or newer (the first to run the site's TypeScript tests unflagged) and pnpm (`check.sh` and the site use the last two).

The Intel release runs under Rosetta with an x86_64 bash 5 that `scripts/build-bash.sh` builds into `~/ely-share/bash-x86_64`.
- Windows: Visual Studio 2022 with the C++ workload (MSVC, a Windows SDK and CMake with Ninja) and clang-cl, from its "C++ Clang tools" component or LLVM in `C:\Program Files\LLVM` (LibreOffice builds Skia with it); gpui compiles its shaders with the SDK's `fxc.exe`. Git for Windows supplies bash and curl. LibreOffice builds under Cygwin in `C:\cygwin64` (`ELY_CYGWIN` elsewhere) with autoconf, automake and LibreOffice's GNU make in `/opt/lo/bin`, as its [Windows build guide](https://wiki.documentfoundation.org/Development/BuildingOnWindows) sets up.
- Linux, one line per family, then pnpm. LibreOffice builds inside `packaging/linux/container.sh`, hence Docker. Ubuntu's own Node.js is too old, so Node.js 22 comes from NodeSource:

```sh
sudo apt install build-essential pkg-config git curl python3 docker.io libdbus-1-dev libfontconfig-dev libxcb1-dev libxkbcommon-x11-dev
curl -fsSL https://deb.nodesource.com/setup_22.x | sudo -E bash - && sudo apt install nodejs

sudo pacman -S --needed base-devel git curl python nodejs npm docker dbus fontconfig libxcb libxkbcommon-x11
sudo npm install -g pnpm
```

`scripts/doctor.sh` checks each of these for the system it runs on.

```sh
scripts/doctor.sh                 # toolchain versions
scripts/fetch-references.sh       # upstream sources at pinned commits
scripts/build-libreoffice.sh      # patched LibreOffice 26.2.6.3 (about an hour)
scripts/build-mupdf.sh            # patched MuPDF 1.28.5
scripts/build-git.sh && scripts/fetch-git-lfs.sh
scripts/fetch-tessdata.sh
cargo build -p ely-lok --bins -p ely-pdf-worker
cargo run -p ely-doc              # or ely-table, ely-show, ely-pdf, ely-mail, ely-tree, ely-mark
```

ElyMail needs a Microsoft client ID at build time: put `ELY_MICROSOFT_CLIENT_ID=<id>` in `cred.txt` at the repository root (git ignores it).

The scripts run on macOS, on Windows (LibreOffice under Cygwin, MuPDF with MSBuild) and on Linux inside `packaging/linux/container.sh`, an AlmaLinux 8 image that keeps the binaries on glibc 2.28.

## Experimental R macros

ElyTable can run local R macros on a selected range, including values, header
formatting and column widths. See [docs/r-macros.md](docs/r-macros.md) for

content.readme:
Airhand

High-performance, low-latency remote desktop
QUIC transport · hardware encoding and decoding · up to 120 fps
Windows · macOS · Linux · Android · browser

English · 简体中文

--- Airhand is a **high-performance, low-latency** remote desktop: the screen is encoded on the GPU (AV1 / HEVC / H.264) at up to 120 fps and sent over QUIC; when the network slows down it skips to the latest frame instead of letting lag pile up; and the mouse pointer is drawn locally, so it moves without delay. The same program is both the **host** (the device being controlled) and the **controller** (the device you control it from). The two sides meet through a **relay server** that you deploy yourself. It's small, and Docker Compose deploys it with one command. Enter the other side's 6-digit **control code** to connect. > [!NOTE] > **Work in progress (0.2.3).** Since protocol v9, client ⇄ server and host ⇄ controller each support a range of versions, new features are negotiated with capability bits and unknown messages are skipped, so later versions can be mixed; versions before v9 are incompatible, which is detected and reported (see [Protocol versions](docs/development.md#protocol-versions)). ## Performance Every stage from capture to display is built for low latency: - **Hardware encoding and decoding**: the host encodes on the GPU (NVENC / Quick Sync / AMF, VideoToolbox, MediaCodec) in low-latency mode without B-frames; the controller decodes on the GPU (WebCodecs / MediaCodec). Measured with a 4K screen streamed at 1080p, hardware AV1 encoding takes about 7 ms per frame (RTX graphics card) - **The best format**: AV1 > HEVC > H.264, automatically picking the most efficient format both sides support; scaling and color conversion use SIMD, and all buffers are reused - **No lag build-up**: the host limits the bytes in flight (≈ bitrate × (RTT + 50 ms)) and skips to the latest frame on a slow network; the bitrate follows the measured queueing delay and bandwidth on every acknowledgement, backing off within a few hundred milliseconds and recovering gradually - **Direct path**: besides the relay, the two ends punch a direct path through their NATs (on the same LAN, or whenever the NAT isn't symmetric), so video and audio stop detouring through the server; the lower-latency path is picked automatically, and if the direct path breaks the session falls back to the relay without dropping - **QUIC + BBR**: BBR congestion control is steadier than Cubic on lossy networks such as Wi-Fi or long-distance links; control messages, audio and video are queued separately, so mouse input and pings never wait behind a large frame; the relay only forwards bytes and never parses the video - **Decode and show**: the decoder runs in low-latency mode, and each frame is drawn to a desynchronized canvas as soon as it's decoded, without waiting for vsync - **Local pointer**: the remote cursor's shape is mirrored locally, and moving it happens locally - **Low bandwidth**: no frames are sent while the screen is still, so an idle desktop uses almost nothing; sessions that aren't on screen drop to 5 fps See [How it works → Video](docs/architecture.md#video) for details. ## Features - **Windows system service**: the lock screen, the sign-in screen and UAC prompts can be seen and controlled, and the computer can be reached after boot, before anyone signs in - **Fixed control codes**: they survive restarts, upgrades and even server restarts until you change them yourself - **Console**: browser-style tabs to control several computers at once, plus a multi-screen overview to watch them all. Computers you've connected to are saved and reconnect with one click; if one is offline, it connects as soon as it comes back - **Web console**: the controller can also run in Docker and be used from a browser, with nothing to install on the computer you control from - **Android**: control computers and phones from a phone as a trackpad or touchscreen, or share your own screen to get help (you approve each connection by default); watch on a TV with the remote - **Audio**: the host's system audio plays on the controller (Opus + adaptive jitter buffer), with optional A/V sync for watching videos - **Handy tools**: two-way clipboard sync, typing the clipboard as keystrokes, system shortcuts (Win, Alt+Tab, Ctrl+Shift+Esc…), multiple monitors, keyboard lock in fullscreen, quality presets - **Secure by default**: sessions are end-to-end encrypted, so the relay server can't see the screen or keystrokes; the first connection needs the pairing code from the other computer's tray (it never goes through the server), and its identity is recognized afterwards; TLS 1.3 with certificate pinning, brute-force protection for control codes; the host always sees who is connected and can disconnect

On Windows, in PowerShell: ```powershell powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -c "irm https://github.com/emanuele-em/kanzo/releases/latest/download/kanzo-installer.ps1 | iex" ``` Both add Kanzo to your `PATH`, for terminals you open from then on. To use it in the one you installed from, run `source $HOME/.cargo/env` (`env.fish` in fish), or open a new one.
